overview: This map record covers 1000 to 1279 in the Armenian highlands, across several changing political orders. It includes the final decades of the Bagratid kingdom of Ani, followed by Byzantine, Seljuk, Georgian and Mongol rule in different places and periods. The repeated outline and its 1100 to 1200 gap are atlas limitations, not a continuous independent kingdom or an empty century.

periods.title: The final Bagratid decades at Ani
periods.summary: Ani was the capital of an Armenian monarchy already established in the ninth century. Byzantine annexation ended this kingdom in 1045.

periods.title: Changing rulers in the highlands
periods.summary: Byzantine and Seljuk conquests reshaped the region; Georgian influence expanded during the later twelfth century.

periods.title: Georgian and Mongol dominance
periods.summary: Armenian regional lords and communities continued under Georgian and then Mongol overlordship. The map’s 1279 endpoint is not a common date of political collapse.

sections.title: A highland crossroads, not one unchanged kingdom

items.text: A new Bagratid monarchy emerged in the 880s. Its capital moved from Bagaran to Kars and then to Ani in 961. The record’s start at 1000 picks up a kingdom already more than a century old.

Different branches of the ruling family established kingdoms at Kars and Lori, while other Armenian dynasties also claimed royal titles. Ani’s king could bear the title “king of kings,” but the highlands contained multiple courts and competing interests. Family connections did not guarantee political unity.

In 1045, Gagik II of Ani was pressured into surrendering his kingdom to the Byzantine emperor. This ended Ani’s Bagratid monarchy; it did not end Armenian society. The date matters because much of this map interval lies after that royal state had ceased to exist.

The Armenian kingdom of Cilicia developed separately near the Mediterranean, with a king crowned in 1198 or 1199. Its capital at Sis lay outside this imported highland outline. A shared language and religious tradition connected Armenian communities without making their different states interchangeable.

sections.title: Cities, households and the work behind trade

items.text: Ani stood on a defensible plateau above river valleys and grew wealthy through a branch of the Silk Roads. Its remains include houses, a market, fortifications, churches, a mosque and a bridge. These structures accumulated under different rulers: the city was more than a royal monument or a single religious community.

Architects and stoneworkers at Ani brought together Armenian, Georgian and Islamic building traditions. Its surviving religious, domestic and military structures show a long exchange of ideas in design and decoration. The ruined city is an archaeological record of those interactions, rather than a perfectly preserved snapshot of one year.

At Ambroyi village, thirteenth- and fourteenth-century excavated spaces contained clay ovens, storage pits and cooking rubbish. Nearby Arai-Bazarjul caravanserai had closely matching cooking jars and red bowls. Archaeologist Kate Franklin argues that village households helped feed travelers. This evidence straddles the map’s 1279 endpoint.

The same thirteenth- and fourteenth-century caravanserai yielded wheat, barley, millet, fruit remains and chopped animal bones. Franklin interprets the combination as evidence for grain-and-meat dishes, perhaps resembling herisa porridge. That is a reconstruction from rubbish, not a surviving menu; the cooks did not leave recipe cards in the drain.

Small finds from Arai-Bazarjul’s medieval gutters included iron nails, fragments of horse or donkey shoes, needles and beads. Trade required repairs and animal care as well as buying and selling. These thirteenth- and fourteenth-century objects reveal everyday maintenance around the caravan routes.

Excavations at Lore fortress uncovered two bathhouses associated with its eleventh- to thirteenth-century development. One had a heater, bathing area and dressing room. Later builders apparently enlarged the bathing space by taking over part of the dressing room and constructing a replacement: even medieval buildings needed remodeling.

Lore’s second bathhouse stood beside the gorge. A reservoir supplied water, and differences in height allowed it to flow through the bath by gravity. Clay pipes and waterproof surfaces reveal the practical work behind a warm wash. The arrangements belong to this complex, not necessarily to every home.

Getting used water out mattered as much as bringing clean water in. At Lore, the gorge-side location made wastewater disposal easier than at the bathhouse in the citadel’s center. This was useful engineering, although draining toward a gorge was not the same thing as modern wastewater treatment.

Haghpat and Sanahin were important centers of learning during the tenth to thirteenth centuries. Sanahin became known for illuminators and calligraphers: specialists who painted and wrote books by hand. Their work joined education, religious devotion and skilled craft in the same monastic setting.

Sanahin’s library-scriptorium was built in 1063 with funds from Hranush, daughter of King David Anhoghin, under Abbot Dioskoros. Her patronage made a royal woman part of the history of learning. Books and religious valuables were stored in deep niches in the walls, not in modern library stacks.

A medieval Armenian manuscript could preserve a small social history in its colophon, the note recording its creation or ownership. Such notes name scribes, donors and sometimes painters or later owners, and may mention personal or political events. These people help historians see beyond the name of a king.

Bookmaking was physical work as well as scholarship. Medieval Armenian images show paper being polished and texts copied from model books. Such illustrations, some from later centuries than this map interval, help explain the continuing craft tradition. A beautiful page began with prepared materials and many patient movements of the hand.

At Dadivank, a building inscription dated 1211 identifies Grigoris, son of Hassan, as the patron of a hall. Its wording ties a construction project to family identity and remembrance of the donor’s soul. This is a named medieval person asking future visitors to remember him.

A short Armenian sample from that inscription is ՅԻՇԵՑԷՔ, transliterated yišecʿēkʿ, meaning “Remember.” It is the final word of the published Armenian transcription, shown here in modern type rather than copied stone lettering. In context, the donor asks to be remembered in prayer.

Armenian stoneworkers developed khachkars, carved cross stones placed at significant sites and used as grave markers. They turned faith and commemoration into a durable public art. Unlike a book that could be carried away, a standing stone also marked a particular place in the landscape.

ending.text: The Bagratid kingdom of Ani ended in 1045, long before this map record stops. Armenian communities and institutions continued under later rulers. Ani’s decline unfolded over centuries, shaped by conquest, changing trade routes and the 1319 earthquake; the city was not suddenly erased at the map’s 1279 boundary.
